cognate: Two pairs, both in the line: OIr traig/troigh 'foot' ~ Serb trag 'track, footprint' (both said to come from *tregʰ-; the Slavic etymology is uncertain), and OIr teichid/teched 'flee/flight' ~ Serb (u)teći 'run (away), escape' (*tekʷ-; secure, cf. Lith. tekėti, OCS tešti).
drift_or_renewal: *tregʰ- noun drifted differently: Irish 'foot (as body part and unit of distance)', Serbian 'footprint, trace'. The phrase uses it as a minimal unit of movement in both ('not one foot' / 'not one trace').
shared_syntax: Negated clause in which the *tregʰ- noun names the smallest quantity and the *tekʷ- word names the flight. But the structure differs: in Irish the noun is the object of 'carry/give' with the verbal noun 'of flight' in the genitive (ní rucus traig techid 'I have not taken a foot of flight'); in Serbian the noun is a partitive genitive subject of the finite verb 'escapes' (не утече трага 'not a trace escapes').
context: Both martial. Irish: a hero's boast or vow (Fer Diad in the Táin; repeated in later Irish annals and romance) never to take a step of retreat before an enemy. Serbian: an exhortation to overtake the imperial army so that not a trace of the enemy gets away. So the polarity differs: the Irish line is about one's own side never fleeing, the Serbian about the enemy being wiped out. The Irish formula is fixed and attested from Middle Irish to Early Modern Irish. The Serbian line occurs once in Vuk.
phrase: NEG + *tekʷ- 'flee' + *tregʰ- 'foot/track' as the smallest unit of movement: OIr ní beir traig techid ~ Serb не утече трага
note: Low: *tekʷ- is the ordinary verb for 'flee' in both languages, so any 'not a foot/step' idiom would bring in the two roots. The Slavic *tragъ < *tregʰ- etymology is not secure (taken from Wiktionary and my memory, not checked against the scholarly literature). Vuk is late, there is a single Serbian attestation, and its meaning is not the Irish one. I report it as a possible shared figure, not as an established formula.

All 172 bundles have Middle Irish pivots; partners are mostly late Greek prose (Galen, Plutarch, Josephus), Old Norse charters and OHG Notker, and nearly every bundle is empty. One low-confidence claim (BC-36e04). Considered and dropped: BC-bece9, OIr búachaill + tarb ~ Gk βουκόλος + ταῦρος (Aelian, Aesop). The compound cognate is real but the pairing is generic pastoral vocabulary. BC-e28bb, OIr bodar ~ Skt badhira 'deaf' in a moral injunction: the Irish translates Lev 19:14. BC-26928/BC-9e83e, snow and wool similes: from Daniel 7:9 and Ps 147. BC-4021d/BC-efcc5, water does not drown, fire does not burn: Antichrist apocalyptic with no partner parallel.
